Summary: The paper builds a controlled benchmark for writing whole OMIM phenotype entries from exactly the papers the curators cited (100 entries, 2-12 references each, causal gene withheld). One LLM (Claude Opus 5.5) writes every draft under shared guards (ontology-candidate-only HPO IDs, HGNC normalisation, mandatory citation), a claim-level audit with one repair round, and a shared scoring pipeline. The strategies are direct long-context reading, an agentic curator with read/search tools, two extract-then-write pipelines (evidence graph, per-patient case table), recall-then-verify, a memory-only control, and three add-ons (second-hand evidence, learned curation guide, reconciled case database). The primary endpoint is coverage of fixed fact lists derived once from OMIM allelic-variant paragraphs deposited in ClinVar. Main findings: (i) hiding full text of the same papers drops coverage from 77.4% to 31.2% (46 entries), far exceeding any difference between strategies; (ii) reading strategies lie within 47.2-49.1% on 93 entries, with replicate noise of +/-1.0 point, and only the case table is reliably worse, a deficit partly removed by a matched ablation raising extraction effort; (iii) the audit catches 60/60 planted single-fact substitutions but checks fidelity, not correctness, and passes second-hand support; (iv) measurement choices (asymmetric handling of safety-filter stops, per-draft fact splitting) move differences by amounts comparable to the effects. All judgements are by the same model family, with no human validation.
Strengths: Unusually careful experimental control: same model, same papers, same guards, audit and scoring for every strategy, with the generation strategy as the only variable; add-ons are tested against their parent strategy.
Fixed fact lists produced once, without sight of any draft, avoid the denominator drift of per-draft claim splitting; the paper shows quantitatively (2-5 points level shift) why this matters.

The within-paper access manipulation (hiding full text of the same papers, same 2,120 facts) is a clean design that cleanly isolates source access from entry/paper confounds, and the missed-fact attribution (Figure 3) usefully decomposes the shortfall into 'not in available text' versus 'stated but omitted'.

Replicate-noise calibration (three repeats on 30 entries) and paired bootstrap with better/worse/tied counts and sign tests give the reader an honest yardstick; the paper explicitly declines to rank strategies whose differences fall within noise.

The completion/safety-filter handling is thought through, and the paper documents that an asymmetric rule produced a spurious 2.1-point deficit, a transferable measurement lesson for agentic/pipeline comparisons.
Matched ablation separating representation from extraction effort is a good practice rarely seen in pipeline comparisons and changes the interpretation of the case-table deficit.
Exceptionally candid scoping and limitations; numbers in text, tables and figures are internally consistent (e.g. Figure 2 bar counts reproduce 31.2% and 77.4%; Figure 3 totals sum to 6,498 facts).
Built from public resources with release of per-entry drafts, verdicts and scores, which makes the benchmark extensible to other models and strategies.
Weaknesses: No human validation of any judgement: fact lists, fact-presence judgements, audit verdicts, missed-fact attribution and contradiction re-adjudication are all produced by the same model family that wrote the drafts. Given known self-preference effects (which the paper cites), even a small human-annotated sample (e.g. 100-200 fact judgements and audit verdicts, with agreement statistics) would substantially strengthen every quantitative claim. As submitted, the absolute coverage levels and the audit's precision are unverified.

Single model, single family. The central claim that strategies are close 'in this regime' cannot be separated from the specific capabilities of one strong long-context model; a weaker or shorter-context model is exactly where extract-then-write and agentic reading are usually motivated. Without a second model the generality of the main comparative result is unknown, which limits the contribution for a general ML venue.

The headline finding (less source text yields less agreement with curators who read full text) is expected, as the paper itself acknowledges; the novelty lies in its magnitude, which is largely a property of this dataset's open-access profile (19% full text). The strategy comparison, the more ML-relevant contribution, is mostly a null within noise.

Regime chosen makes separation unlikely: entries with 2-12 references whose inputs fit one prompt are the case in which direct long-context reading should be hard to beat. The 30-75-reference tier is exploratory with about ten entries. A benchmark meant to compare reading/extraction strategies would be more informative with inputs that exceed the context window or stress retrieval.

The primary endpoint is narrow and indirect: variant-centred allelic-variant paragraphs, not the entries' narrative sections, and drafts make roughly twice as many statements as the reference has facts, so coverage is a lower bound and draft content beyond the reference is checked only by the self-audit.
Strategies were developed on the evaluation entries, with no separate development set; the 20 post-June-2026 entries partially mitigate this but are few.

Access-experiment asymmetry: the full-text arm went through the repair round while abstract arms did not, and full-text coverage before repair was not scored. The argument that repair moves coverage little is indirect (unsupported-claim counts, not coverage).

Audit evaluation is limited to 60 blunt single-fact substitutions with no unaltered controls, so the false-flag rate is unknown and omission/misattribution errors are untested; 'the audit flagged all 60' therefore says little about practical audit reliability.

Fit to ICLR: methodologically there is no new learning method or representation; the contribution is a domain benchmark plus measurement practice. That is acceptable for ICLR's datasets/benchmarks area, but then the benchmark's validity (human-validated reference matching, judge validation) needs to be stronger than it is here.

Presentation density: the main text is packed with numbers and qualifiers, many results are deferred to an extensive appendix (Tables 2-18, Appendix I), and the abstract groups the memory-only control with 'memory-first strategies'. Figure 4 axis labels and annotations are very small in print.
Questions: Can you provide any human validation, even on a small random sample: agreement between a domain expert and the model on fact presence (present/partly/absent/contradicted), on audit verdicts, and on the quality of the fixed fact splits? What agreement would you consider sufficient for the coverage numbers to be trusted?
Have you run even a subset (e.g. the 30 replicate entries) with a second model family, either as writer or as judge? If the judge is swapped, do the strategy orderings and the access effect persist?

Figure 2 coverages appear to be pooled over facts (e.g. (1513+254/2)/2120 = 77.4%), whereas the primary endpoint is defined as a per-entry mean. Which is reported in the abstract and Section 4.1, and do the two agree?
What is full-text-arm coverage before repair in the access experiment? Since drafts are cached, scoring the pre-repair full-text draft seems cheap and would remove the asymmetry.

How often was the safety filter triggered per strategy, and is triggering correlated with entry content (e.g. specific disease categories)? Could this induce selection effects on the 93-entry comparison set?

For abstract-only papers, direct reading conveys 40.1% of facts while only 2% of missed facts were stated in the abstract. Can you estimate cued recall by, e.g., giving the model a shuffled or mismatched abstract, or by restricting to facts verifiably absent from the abstract?

Do the strategies separate on inputs that exceed one prompt? A small experiment on the larger-reference tier with chunked direct reading vs. extract-then-write would directly test where intermediate representations help.
How were the strategies' prompts tuned on the evaluation entries, and how much effort went into each? Could unequal development effort explain the case-table gap independently of extraction effort?
Limitations: The authors list limitations thoroughly (single model family, no human validation, indirect reference, open-access-only text, given reference lists, development on evaluation entries, safety-filter losses, unmeasured audit false-flag rate). The most consequential, the absence of any human validation of the model judges, is acknowledged but not mitigated.
Generalisation beyond small entries that fit one prompt and beyond one model is untested.
Generated entries are explicitly framed as drafts for expert review, not clinical guidance, which is appropriate.
Thought: Very carefully controlled and honest study; internal numbers check out (Fig. 2 bar counts reproduce the coverages, Fig. 3 totals = 6,498). But every measurement is a same-family model judgement with zero human validation, only one model was tested, the regime (small entries fitting in one prompt) makes strategy differences unlikely, and the main positive finding (full text >> abstract) is expected. Strategy comparison is essentially a null within replicate noise. As an ICLR benchmark paper it needs judge validation and at least a second model to support its claims beyond this specific setup. Leaning reject but persuadable with human validation and a second model.
